narrative: The model estimated your chance of failing the final year at 11%, or roughly one in nine. That is a low probability, not a certainty, but under the rule used for this decision it was enough to flag you for remedial courses as a precaution. The strongest factor in your profile was that you have no past class failures—exactly the average for students who passed—which worked in your favor. Next came the quality of your family relationships: yours are rated good, which is common among passing students and also pushed your risk down. Third was your wish to pursue higher education; every passing student in this comparison wanted to continue, so this goal counted toward passing. These top three influences were therefore protective: they are not reasons you are likely to fail, but reasons your estimated risk is not higher. The 11% flag comes from the combined effect of other, less influential details rather than from these main factors. To improve, keep protecting the strengths the model noticed: avoid any subject failures, lean on your good family support, and keep your higher-education goal clear. Use the remedial courses to strengthen study routines, especially by adding more structured weekly study beyond the current two-to-five hours, and ask for help early if a subject becomes difficult. Your zero absences and existing school and family support are also useful advantages to maintain.
